summary: Defines a CERT resource record so certificates and related certificate revocation lists can be stored in the Domain Name System. It obsoletes RFC 2538. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: The internet's phone book can also hold ID badges, so you can look one up by name.

how to store certificates in dns

subtitle: The CERT record: a DNS resource record type for storing certificates and revocation lists.

tldr.problem: Public keys are published as certificates, and there was a need to store those certificates and revocation lists in the Domain Name System where they can be looked up by name.
tldr.mechanism: A CERT resource record (RR type 37) carries a certificate type, a key tag, an algorithm number and the certificate or CRL, with rules for which owner names to store it under.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2538, adds an IANA registry of certificate types, and defines indirect types that point to a URL when the data is too large. It has since been updated by RFC 6944.

facts.label: Indirect types
facts.value: IPKIX, ISPKI, IPGP, IACPKIX (4 to 6 and 8)

today: RFC 4398 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2538 and has been updated by RFC 6944.

sections.title: Certificates in the DNS
sections.content:
A certificate binds a public key to identity or authorization information through a cryptographic digital signature. A certificate revocation list (CRL) lists certificates that have been revoked, signed by their issuer. The RFC gives X.509 and OpenPGP certificates as examples.

RFC 4398 defines a CERT resource record for storing such certificates and CRLs in the Domain Name System, and discusses what owner names to use. It obsoletes RFC 2538, and the RFC states that the majority of its text is copied verbatim from RFC 2538.
sections.eli5: A certificate is like an ID badge that proves a key belongs to someone. This RFC says how to keep badges in the internet's phone book.

sections.title: The CERT Resource Record
sections.content:
The CERT RR has RR type code 37. Its data has four parts: a 16-bit type, a 16-bit key tag, an 8-bit algorithm, and the certificate or CRL itself.

The key tag is computed for the key embedded in the certificate using the RRSIG Key Tag algorithm. It is an efficiency measure: a client can compute the tag for its key and examine only CERT RRs with the same tag. Two different keys can share a tag. The key must first be transformed into the form of the public key part of a DNSKEY RR. If that is not possible, the algorithm field MUST be zero and the tag SHOULD be zero.

The algorithm field has the same meaning as in DNSKEY and RRSIG RRs, except that zero means the algorithm is unknown to a secure DNS.

In the text (master file) form, the type and algorithm can be decimal integers or mnemonics, the key tag is a decimal integer, and the certificate is base 64, which may be split into white-space-separated pieces.
sections.eli5: Each entry has a label saying what kind of badge it is, a short number to help find the right one quickly, a note on the lock type used, and then the badge itself.

sections.title: Certificate Type Values
sections.content:
The type field selects the format of what follows. The main types are PKIX (1, an X.509 certificate conforming to the PKIX profile), SPKI (2, reserved), PGP (3, an OpenPGP packet) and ACPKIX (7, an attribute certificate). OpenPGP data is binary and MUST NOT be ASCII armored.

Four indirect types hold a URL instead of the data: IPKIX (4), ISPKI (5), IPGP (6) and IACPKIX (8). They MUST be used when the content is too large for the record and MAY be used at the implementer's discretion. They SHOULD NOT be used where the DNS message is 512 octets or smaller and could thus be expected to fit a UDP packet. IPGP holds a one-octet fingerprint length, the OpenPGP fingerprint, and then the URL; either the fingerprint or the URL may be empty, but not both.

Types 253 (URI) and 254 (OID) are private formats. A URI type begins with a null-terminated URI. An OID type begins with a one-octet OID length and then a BER-encoded OID. Conforming PKIX certificates SHOULD use the PKIX type rather than the OID type.
sections.eli5: Some entries hold the badge itself. If the badge is too big for the entry, the entry holds the address of where to fetch it instead.

sections.title: Choosing Owner Names
sections.content:
A certificate CERT RR should be stored under a domain name related to its subject. A CRL CERT RR should be stored under a name related to its issuer. The RFC defines two styles. A content-based owner name is derived from the certificate's content, such as the X.509 Subject or the OpenPGP User ID. A purpose-based owner name is one a client would already know, such as the hostname of a TLS server or a Key ID.

Implementations SHOULD use the purpose-based guidelines and MAY use CNAME records at content-based names (or other names) pointing to the purpose-based name.

  • S/MIME: the standard translation of the email address, so postmaster@example.org becomes postmaster.example.org.
  • TLS: the hostname of the server.
  • IPsec: the hostname of the machine, or for addresses the fully qualified name in the reverse domain.
  • OpenPGP: the key fingerprint, the key ID, or the translated email address, using CNAME to avoid duplicating the key.

For content-based X.509 names, the RFC gives a priority order: a domain name in the certificate, then the inverse domain name of an IP address, then a domain name inside a URI, then a character string name treated like an OpenPGP name, and finally the distinguished name mapped to a domain name. The DNS itself infers no relationship among CERT records from their owner names.
sections.eli5: To find a badge you need to know which name it is filed under. The RFC suggests filing it under a name people already know, such as a website's name or an email address.

sections.title: Size and Performance
sections.content:
The DNS was designed for small transfers, typically below 512 octets. Larger transfers work, but every reasonable effort should be made to keep stored certificates small, for example by using few optional fields and short values.

The RDATA field of a DNS record can hold only 65535 octets (64kb) or less. A CERT RR therefore MUST NOT contain more than 64kb of payload, even if the certificate or CRL is larger, which is why the indirect types exist.

The RFC also warns that using CERT RRs for signed email moves lookups from per-domain to per-user. If deployed widely, this may raise DNS load, though whether the increase would be noticeable is not known.
sections.eli5: The phone book works best with short entries. Very big badges are stored elsewhere, and the entry just says where.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Certificates carry their own signatures, so it is reasonable to store them in non-secure DNS zones or fetch them without DNS security checking. The result may be trusted if the certificate chain is verified back to a known trusted key and this fits the user's policy. If certificates come from a secure zone with DNS security checking, the key may be trusted without verifying the chain, again if policy allows.

  • With DNSSEC using NSEC, an organization that publishes employee certificates could let someone enumerate all of its employees.
  • The URI type adds an indirection that may open a new vulnerability. One way to secure it is to include a hash of the certificate in the URI.
  • With DNSSEC, the non-existence of a CERT RR can be securely asserted. Without it, this is not possible.
sections.eli5: A badge proves itself with its stamp, so it is fine to keep it in a public book. But a list of everyone's badges could reveal who works somewhere.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Changes
sections.content:
IANA created a registry of CERT RR certificate types. Values 0, 255 and 65535 are reserved. Values 9 to 252 are available by IETF Standards action, 256 to 65279 by IETF Consensus, and 65280 to 65534 are for experimental use. The CERT RR also reuses the DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry and requires that algorithm number 0 stay reserved.

Compared to RFC 2538, this document replaces KEY/SIG with DNSKEY/RRSIG terminology, uses OpenPGP in place of PGP, clarifies that OpenPGP data is binary, adds CNAME examples, adds purpose-based owner names and size considerations, reserves the SPKI types, adds the four indirect types, and creates the IANA registry.
sections.eli5: A keeper of the list hands out new badge-kind numbers, and some number ranges are held back for private or experimental use.

smith        IN CERT PGP 0 0 <OpenPGP binary>
john.smith   IN CNAME smith
